prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Polygamist sect leader Warren Jeffs tried to hang himself earlier this year while he was in jail awaiting trial, according to court documents unsealed by a Utah judge on Tuesday. Sect leader Warren Jeffs arrives in court to hear the verdict against him September 25 in St. George, Utah. Jeffs, the leader and so-called prophet of the 10,000-member Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, is now awaiting sentencing after being convicted on two counts of being an accomplice to rape. The documents, released by Fifth District Judge James Shumate at the request of the media, also indicate that Jeffs confessed to "immorality" with a "sister" and a daughter more than 30 years ago. Among the documents is a competency report on Jeffs completed in April, in which social worker Eric Nielsen wrote that throughout the month of January, Jeffs refused food and drink and developed ulcers on his knees from kneeling in prayer for hours. On January 28, the report said, he attempted to hang himself in his cell. In the days following the suicide attempt, while he was on suicide watch, Jeffs on separate occasions threw himself against the wall and banged his head on the wall. Jail transcripts show that Jeffs' suicide attempt came three days after a visit with his brother, Nephi, in which he said, "I am not the prophet. I never was the prophet, and I have been deceived by the powers of evil ... I ask for everyone's forgiveness." Jeffs also told his brother: "Farewell forever." The day before that, Jeffs told a follower in a phone conversation that he was "covered with immorality with a sister and a daughter when I was younger." In the FLDS, members call adult women "sister," and Jeffs' meaning was unclear. Jeffs' defense attorneys, who argued against the release of the documents, said in a motion opposing the unsealing of the statements that Jeffs recanted them the following month. Defense attorneys claim Jeffs' medical condition influenced his state of mind when the statements were made. They presented Shumate with a letter from another Jeffs attorney, arguing that the statements' release could influence an Arizona jury when Jeffs stands trial in that state. Jeffs, 51, was convicted in September of being an accomplice to rape. He was accused of using his religious influence over his followers to coerce a 14-year-old girl into marriage to her 19-year-old cousin. He faces a sentence of up to life in prison when he is sentenced November 20. The FLDS -- which is not affiliated with the mainstream Mormon church -- is based in the side-by-side border towns of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona. Jeffs, a former school headmaster, is the son of the sect's previous president and "prophet," Rulon Jeffs, who died in 2002. Jeffs was on the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives list when he was arrested in August 2006 outside Las Vegas, Nevada. Critics say that inside the FLDS, marriages are arranged for girls as young as 13, and competition for brides may be reduced by exiling male teens and young men. If male followers are excommunicated, critics claim, wives and children can be reassigned. During Jeffs' trial, defense attorneys claimed authorities were persecuting Jeffs because of his religious beliefs, including practicing polygamy as the way to heaven. If Jeffs disavowed being the prophet of the FLDS, it could cause upheaval within the secretive sect. However, two of his followers who spoke to CNN -- although FLDS members usually do not talk to reporters -- said they do not believe he made the statements. "He is a perfectly priestly man," said a woman who identified herself as Cathy. "He is a man of God, and we will always love him. Once a prophet, always a prophet." Her husband, Patrick, told CNN, "It's hogwash. I don't believe it ... I will always consider him my prophet." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Gary Tuchman contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**(CNN) —** Polygamist sect leader Warren Jeffs attempted to hang himself earlier this year while jailed awaiting trial, according to court documents unsealed Tuesday by a Utah judge.

*Sect leader Warren Jeffs arrives in court to hear the verdict against him on September 25 in St. George, Utah.*

Jeffs, the leader and self-proclaimed prophet of the 10,000-member Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, is awaiting sentencing after being convicted on two counts of being an accomplice to rape.

The documents, released by Fifth District Judge James Shumate at the media’s request, also indicate that Jeffs confessed to “immorality” with a “sister” and a daughter more than 30 years ago.

Among the documents is a competency report on Jeffs completed in April. In it, social worker Eric Nielsen wrote that throughout January, Jeffs refused food and drink and developed ulcers on his knees after kneeling in prayer for hours.

According to the report, Jeffs attempted to hang himself in his cell on January 28. In the days following the suicide attempt, while under suicide watch, he separately threw himself against a wall and banged his head against it.

Jail transcripts show that Jeffs’ suicide attempt occurred three days after a visit with his brother, Nephi, during which he said: “I am not the prophet. I never was the prophet, and I have been deceived by the powers of evil ... I ask for everyone’s forgiveness.”

Jeffs also told his brother, “Farewell forever.”

The previous day, Jeffs told a follower during a phone conversation that he was “covered with immorality with a sister and a daughter when I was younger.”

Within the FLDS, members refer to adult women as “sister,” and Jeffs’ meaning was unclear.

Jeffs’ defense attorneys, who opposed the documents’ release, said in a motion seeking to keep the statements sealed that Jeffs recanted them the following month. They maintain that Jeffs’ medical condition affected his state of mind when he made the statements.

The defense also presented Shumate with a letter from another of Jeffs’ attorneys arguing that releasing the statements could influence an Arizona jury when Jeffs stands trial in that state.

Jeffs, 51, was convicted in September of being an accomplice to rape. He was accused of using his religious influence over his followers to coerce a 14-year-old girl into marrying her 19-year-old cousin. He faces a sentence of up to life in prison when he is sentenced on November 20.

The FLDS, which is not affiliated with the mainstream Mormon Church, is based in the neighboring border towns of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona.

Jeffs, a former school headmaster, is the son of the sect’s previous president and “prophet,” Rulon Jeffs, who died in 2002. He was on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list when he was arrested outside Las Vegas, Nevada, in August 2006.

Critics say that within the FLDS, marriages are arranged for girls as young as 13 and that competition for brides may be reduced by exiling teenage boys and young men. They also claim that when male followers are excommunicated, their wives and children can be reassigned.

During Jeffs’ trial, defense attorneys argued that authorities were persecuting him because of his religious beliefs, including the practice of polygamy as the path to heaven.

If Jeffs were to disavow his role as prophet of the FLDS, it could cause upheaval within the secretive sect. However, two of his followers who spoke with CNN—although FLDS members generally do not speak to reporters—said they did not believe he had made the statements.

“He is a perfectly priestly man,” said a woman who identified herself as Cathy. “He is a man of God, and we will always love him. Once a prophet, always a prophet.”

Her husband, Patrick, told CNN: “It’s hogwash. I don’t believe it ... I will always consider him my prophet.”

*E-mail to a friend.*

CNN’s Gary Tuchman contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Court records made public Tuesday by a Utah judge reveal that Warren Jeffs, the head of a polygamous religious sect, attempted suicide by hanging while jailed earlier this year and waiting to go on trial.

Jeffs appeared in court in St. George, Utah, on September 25 to hear the verdict against him. The 51-year-old leader and self-described prophet of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, which has about 10,000 members, is awaiting sentencing after a jury found him guilty on two charges of acting as an accomplice to rape.

Fifth District Judge James Shumate released the records in response to requests from news organizations. The material also says Jeffs admitted to committing “immorality” with a “sister” and a daughter more than three decades earlier.

One of the documents is an April evaluation of Jeffs’ competency. In it, social worker Eric Nielsen reported that Jeffs went without food and liquids throughout January and developed sores on his knees after spending hours kneeling in prayer.

According to the report, Jeffs tried to hang himself in his jail cell on January 28. While under suicide watch afterward, he repeatedly hurled himself into a wall and struck his head against it on separate occasions.

Transcripts from the jail indicate that the attempt occurred three days after Jeffs met with his brother Nephi. During that visit, Jeffs said he was not—and had never been—the prophet, that evil forces had misled him, and that he wanted everyone to forgive him. He also gave his brother what he described as a permanent farewell.

A day before that meeting, Jeffs told a follower by telephone that, when he was younger, he had been “covered with immorality with a sister and a daughter.” Because adult women in the FLDS are addressed as “sister,” the precise meaning of his statement was uncertain.

Jeffs’ lawyers opposed making the records public. In their motion against unsealing the statements, they said he withdrew them the next month. The defense maintained that his physical condition had affected his thinking when he made the remarks.

They also submitted to Shumate a letter from another attorney representing Jeffs. It argued that public disclosure could prejudice jurors in Arizona, where Jeffs is also expected to be tried.

Jeffs was convicted in September of serving as an accomplice to rape. Prosecutors accused him of exploiting his religious authority to pressure a 14-year-old girl into marrying her 19-year-old cousin. At his November 20 sentencing, he could receive a prison term of up to life.

The FLDS has no connection to the mainstream Mormon church. Its headquarters are in the neighboring border communities of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona.

Before leading the sect, Jeffs worked as a school headmaster. His father, Rulon Jeffs, had previously served as the group’s president and “prophet” until his death in 2002.

Jeffs was included on the FBI’s list of 10 most-wanted fugitives when authorities arrested him near Las Vegas, Nevada, in August 2006.

According to critics of the FLDS, the sect arranges marriages involving girls as young as 13. They also allege that teenage boys and young men may be expelled to reduce rivalry for prospective wives. Critics further claim that when male members are excommunicated, their wives and children may be assigned to someone else.

During the Utah trial, Jeffs’ attorneys argued that officials were targeting him because of his faith, including the belief that plural marriage is a path to heaven.

Any rejection by Jeffs of his role as FLDS prophet could destabilize the highly secretive organization. Nevertheless, two followers who spoke with CNN—despite the fact that FLDS members rarely speak to journalists—said they did not accept that he had made the reported comments.

A woman who gave her name as Cathy described Jeffs as entirely priestly and as a man of God whom followers would always love. She said that someone who becomes a prophet remains one permanently.

Her husband, Patrick, dismissed the reports as nonsense, saying he did not believe them and would continue to regard Jeffs as his prophet.

The original CNN page included an option to e-mail the report to a friend. CNN’s Gary Tuchman contributed to the story.

Jeffs, the leader of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, was being held on charges stemming from his role in arranging a marriage involving an underage girl. He was later convicted as an accomplice to rape and is awaiting sentencing.

According to the newly released records, Jeffs’ behavior in custody became increasingly troubling. He engaged in prolonged fasting and prayer, at times appearing withdrawn and despondent. Jail and medical personnel monitored him as concerns grew about his health and safety. Those disclosures come as the court prepares to sentence him following his conviction, adding a new and complicated dimension to a case that has drawn national attention to Jeffs and the secretive polygamist community he led.
